‘Oh, it’s nothing! I enjoy it. Money isn’t why I work; my art is everything to me.’

Lord Arthur placed four pounds, two shillings and sixpence on the table, thanked the little German for his kindness, and, after managing to turn down an invitation to meet some Anarchists over a substantial tea the next Saturday, left the house and headed for the Park.

He spent the following two days intensely excited, and at noon on Friday drove to the Buckingham to wait for news. Throughout the afternoon the impassive hall porter continued to put up telegrams from different parts of the country reporting race results, divorce verdicts, weather conditions, and similar matters. Meanwhile, the ticker delivered tedious particulars of an overnight session in the House of Commons and a minor panic on the Stock Exchange. The evening papers arrived at four, and Lord Arthur retreated into the library carrying the Pall Mall, the St. James’s, the Globe, and the Echo. This deeply offended Colonel Goodchild, who was eager to read accounts of the speech he had given that morning at the Mansion House about South African Missions and the desirability of appointing black Bishops in every province, and who, for some reason, strongly disliked the Evening News. Yet none of these papers made even a passing reference to Chichester, and Lord Arthur concluded that the attempt had failed. The disappointment was devastating, and for a while he lost his composure entirely. He visited Herr Winckelkopf the following day and received profuse apologies, together with an offer of another clock at no charge, or a case of nitroglycerine bombs at cost. But Lord Arthur’s faith in explosives had vanished, and Herr Winckelkopf himself admitted that so many products were adulterated these days that even pure dynamite was almost impossible to obtain. Although the little German conceded that something must have malfunctioned in the mechanism, he still hoped the clock might explode. He cited a barometer he had once sent the military Governor of Odessa: set to go off after ten days, it had waited something like three months before exploding. Admittedly, when it finally did explode, its only achievement was to blow a housemaid to pieces, since the Governor had left town six weeks earlier. Nevertheless, the incident at least demonstrated that dynamite, when its destructive power was governed by machinery, remained a potent force, even if it could not always be relied on for punctuality.

Count Rouvaloff regarded him in astonishment for a little while; then, perceiving that he meant what he said, he put an address on a scrap of paper, added his initials, and passed it over the table.

‘Scotland Yard would pay handsomely for that address, my dear fellow.’

‘They won’t get it,’ exclaimed Lord Arthur with a laugh; and, having clasped the young Russian’s hand warmly, he hurried downstairs, glanced at the paper, and directed his coachman to Soho Square.

He dismissed the man there and wandered along Greek Street until he reached a place named Bayle’s Court. Going beneath its arch, he entered a singular cul-de-sac which appeared to house a French Laundry: clothes-lines formed an intricate web between the houses, and white linen fluttered in the morning breeze. He went to the far end and knocked on the door of a small green house. There was a pause, in which every window about the court filled with an indistinct crowd of inquisitive faces; at last a somewhat rough-featured foreigner opened the door and in exceedingly poor English demanded his business. Lord Arthur offered him the paper from Count Rouvaloff. At sight of it the man bowed and ushered him into a very shabby front sitting-room on the ground floor. Presently Herr Winckelkopf, as England knew him, hurried in with a napkin much stained by wine fastened about his neck, and a fork held in his left hand.

‘Count Rouvaloff has furnished me with an introduction,’ Lord Arthur said with a bow, ‘and I should like a brief interview concerning a business matter. I am Smith, Mr. Robert Smith, and I wish you to provide me with an explosive clock.’

‘Delighted to meet you, Lord Arthur,’ replied the amiable little German, laughing. ‘Pray don’t seem so frightened; knowing everyone is my business, and I recollect seeing you one evening at Lady Windermere’s. I trust her ladyship is well. Will you join me while I finish breakfast? The pâté is excellent, and my friends flatter me that my Rhine wine surpasses anything served at the German Embassy.’ Before Lord Arthur could recover from the surprise of recognition, he was sitting in the back-room, tasting a most exquisite Marcobrünner from a pale-yellow hock-glass bearing the Imperial monogram, and conversing with the celebrated conspirator on the most friendly terms.

‘Explosive clocks,’ Herr Winckelkopf observed, ‘are rather unsuitable articles to send abroad. Even when they manage to get through the Custom House, the railway service is so uncertain that they generally explode before arriving at their intended destination.

The neighbouring oaks sheltered a colony of nightingales—there I stand again; Idris is beside me, in the sweet spring of youth—remember that I am but twenty-two, and the beloved of my soul has scarcely seen seventeen summers. Swelled by the autumn rains, the river had overflowed the low ground, and Adrian, aboard his favourite boat, pursues the perilous amusement of gathering the highest branch of a flooded oak. Have you grown tired of living, O Adrian, that danger is your plaything?—

His trophy won, he guides his little vessel through the inundation. We watched him with anxious eyes, but the current swept him away from us; he must come ashore much farther down, and travel a long circuit before reaching us. ‘He is safe!’ Idris exclaimed when he sprang to land and flourished his branch above his head in triumph; ‘let us await him here.’

We stood alone together; the sun was gone, the nightingales had begun their singing, and the evening star gleamed clearly amid the sea of brightness still lingering in the western sky. My angelic girl’s blue eyes rested upon that gentle image of herself. ‘How its light throbs,’ she said, ‘that light which gives the star its life! The unsteady radiance seems to tell us that its condition, like our own on earth, is changeful and uncertain; I think it fears, and loves.’

‘Do not watch the star, my dear and noble friend,’ I cried; ‘do not decipher love in its quivering beams. Turn from those remote worlds, and speak no more of a feeling merely fancied. Long have I kept silence; long, until the longing sickened me, have I wished to speak and place my soul, my life, my whole existence in your keeping. Look not at the star, beloved—or look, and allow that everlasting spark to plead my cause; let its silent shining bear witness and speak for me. Love is to me what light is to that star; as long as annihilation has not quenched it, so long shall my love endure.’

The rapture of that instant must remain for ever hidden from the world’s unfeeling gaze. Still I feel her lovely form against my overflowing heart—still my sight, my pulse, my very breath grow faint and fail as I recall that earliest kiss. In silence, slowly, we moved to meet Adrian, whose approach we heard.

I begged Adrian to come back to me when he had escorted his sister home. That very evening, as we walked the forest paths beneath the moon, I emptied my heart before my friend, with all its joy and expectation. For an instant a troubled look crossed his face. ‘I ought to have foreseen it,’ he said; ‘what contention must follow now!’
